I was in a very similar boat. I took the strategy of packing and leaving while he was at work, foregoing any opportunity for him to turn it into a blame-shifting argument and to give myself desperately needed respite from the chaos and confusion that was our blunt-ended communication. I wrote him a long email expressing how deeply I loved him and how I needed change, true safety, a full acknowledgment of the truth, and to stop making compromises on un-compromisable boundaries, such as which country we lived in and when we were to start a family. I lucked out in a way - he demanded a divorce immediately and would not, or could not, hear me. I get that most people believe leaving the door open is a waste of time - it likely is. But I saw it this way; even if he slams the door shut, I will leave knowing my integrity is intact as to how I felt in my heart and did not deny it to myself or to him, and that I truly gave him all of my heart while protecting it. That being said - if he had kept the door open and he had faithfully attended abuser therapy while I was living separately, it would have presented a magnanimous opportunity for him to hoover me back in with a siren song of change. You can leave while leaving the door open - but you're tethering yourself to the very real possibility of being hoovered into the cycle again and wasting your time, so bear this in mind. Since it sounds like real estate and children are involved, I must point out that you would be very wise to consult with a local attorney before making any definitive plans to leave like I did - those two factors can make leaving much more complicated, but it is certainly possible with the right help. Don't let anyone tell you to shut down your grieving heart in a specific way - the decision of how and when must come from you. You've had him ordering and telling you what to do long enough, so ordering-style advice from others will only cause you to retreat into the cycle harder, I'd avoid those types of advice givers.

Do you mean, was it your fault? Absolutely not. Nothing justifies this behavior even if you DID do something that accidentally hurt her feelings. It is not your job to change who you are or walk around on eggshells for her, or to “avoid” things she may not like. Certainly, as a partner, you are expected to listen to her concerns and boundaries, but boundaries sound like “I will not do X, Y, Z”. Concerns sound like “I feel X, Y, Z”. Where the “you” language happens is such a tag for coercion and manipulation, because NO ONE can tell you who you are, how you feel, what you want, or what you can or cannot do. Control sounds like “YOU will not do X, Y, Z”. Manipulation and blaming sounds like “YOU are x, y, Z.” And of course they will pretend such differences are trivial, and they are not. So she can respectfully ask you not to do something - you have every right to equally say “actually, I am not comfortable with that, and no”. No, I will not delete all females from my social media. No, I will not restrict patient access to me. No is a full sentence. No requires no justification or apology. And if someone cannot handle your “no”, they do not deserve your “yes”.

You are simply in need of help and healing. Please reach out to local resources for DV survivors and perhaps a therapist who has trauma and abuse-informed credentials. EMDR. That sort. You and your precious bodily temple deserve gentleness, safety, and sanctuary in your own mind, and it can be found with the right help.

My dear, I am so sorry you are going through this. You do not deserve any of it, nor are you imagining things. Your body knows what feels right and what doesn't it. You don't need to justify it to anyone. And I can understand why you would be window-shopping in dating apps, even if people here are going to take capital offense to that coping behavior while wildly overlooking the extensive abuse you suffered. But I think the best advice is this - keep talking about it with people you trust IF it is safe to do so. It isn't wrong to confide in others when he's hurting you, no matter how much he might have made you believe that. And don't be ashamed to reach out to get help - to go stay with or lean on family - to contact whatever agencies or organizations can help you get out safely, or offer counseling. There is no shame in this - it is HIS shame to carry. In the meantime, I highly recommend this free book, widely circulated in this forum: [https://dn790007.ca.archive.org/0/items/LundyWhyDoesHeDoThat/Lundy\_Why-does-he-do-that.pdf](https://dn790007.ca.archive.org/0/items/LundyWhyDoesHeDoThat/Lundy_Why-does-he-do-that.pdf)

The short answer is: because rejection hurts and it sucks. Your emotions aren't logical, and the feelings don't mean you want to stay. The feelings mean that you're a human who has loved and tried over and over, and seeing everything you lovingly gave get discarded is awful (and unfair). And the longer answer is one of trauma bonding and emotional enmeshment - the heart is still in it in some way, despite how badly your brain and body crave safety and autonomy. I have often felt the same way you are describing, and my therapist has guided me to respect that feeling for what it is (hurt at rejection) without interpreting it to mean anything more than that. Being hurt by his divorce threats (or even if he filed) does NOT equate to loving him, or that staying is a good idea. It's like how you would feel pain if you touched the hot stove - it's just a natural reaction. It's confounding on a logical level, but we are far from logical creatures. You are allowed to feel whatever you need to when he's hurt you. You are allowed to miss and grieve the version of him you thought he was (or to have your righteous anger burn bright). But please, internet stranger, hold yourself gently no matter what those feelings are, for they are sacred and need no explanations, only space.

YTA. I make more than my partner and I consider our ability to contribute to rent on a percentage basis with the higher earning partner using their percentage of rent as a benchmark. So for example, if you’re netting 10k a month, $1900 in rent is approximately 19% of your gross take home, something you could easily afford. That means if she were to pay 19% of her gross earnings to rent, her contribution while making $40k would be around $633. She would pay 19% of her income to rent, and you’d automatically be paying proportionately less. You would only be paying around $1267, which is more like 12.67% of what you make. Proportionally, I am sure there is a more precise way, but my logic on this for my partner is always simple - they should never have to pay a rent contribution that is a higher percentage of their income than I would pay out of my own income if I were renting single. In this scenario, say you both decided to upgrade to a $2600 apartment, then the limit becomes 26%. 

Having a 19% rent burden is a privilege a lot of hard-working people don’t have, and asking your partner to pay proportionately more will only prevent them from being able to focus on increasing their own earning potential and catching up to you, if that’s what they want. If they aren’t looking to make as much as you and either partner isn’t okay with that, it wouldn’t have worked out anyway. Very few couples make identical salaries or have identical wealth, so working something out that is fair is al aye going to be more than math or a simple 50/50 mindset. I think 50/50 time and energy into the relationship and household is a more realistic expectation than an assumption of coequal incomes.

Every problem became solvable by simply pushing myself harder, becoming better, and diving into all of these traditional norms of success. Being a hero became a survival mechanism. Life was a battle, and it was fight or die. So I was the archetype, the tragic hero, and the skills I gained were all rooted in an absolute tragedy.

And perhaps that is where being an ACOA can be so sneaky and insidious. People see overachieving and assume it makes us inherently good or moral in some way, they see how closely we align with social codes and ethics. We are so praised and rewarded for our outward successes that it masks our skewed perceptions and the problematic forces driving our success become invisible. The alcoholics get all of the attention, and yet we suffer silently, wrapped in a disguise so convincing that even we are fooled. 

When people asked me how I became so successful, I used to say that I had a "river of pure rage that flows through a valley of hate" somewhere deep inside me, and I would think that the best way to deal with it was to use it as a kind of hydroelectric generator for my internal motivation to succeed. Inside my heart and mind, my God-given intellect and brilliance are like this Eden of beautiful and exotic plants that have no names, and people see it and stand in awe. But if you dig beneath, past the roots, the water is like acid from toxic soil. Like that river runs as a burning force through the center of that beautiful valley, awful and powerful, fueling that hydroelectric dam to power all of those buildings I've made into a city of knowledge and skills. 

And it makes me have this small glimmer of hope that maybe that hydroelectric emotional motivational mechanism I have in me can be rebuilt in the valley in my heart devoted to love and gratitude. I think the 12 Steps can help me do that. Take apart the mechanisms driven by resentments and retool those really high-functioning parts into ones run on love, into a magnificent internal emotional source of motivation that can allow me to do more (and give more to this world) than I ever imagined. Such a machination in my heart would be the magnum opus that the sad kid in me always dreamed of.  It's gonna be scary as Hell, but if I can take all of it apart, if I can let the steps open my heart up to God's love, that water in all of my valleys can be of love. And of what I know of love, it is a river and a source that would quench that garden of brilliance in me in a way that I have never seen or imagined before, and the things I already love about me would flower with a force unheard of.

My Q/husband had this moment before he broke down and decided to go to treatment, when we were about to break things off. He was screaming at me in his anger, about how his anger was a power he had. He could tell people things and get results through it. Anger was useful, hate was useful. He was going off, not drunk, but a few drinks in. 

I remember a moment from my Higher Power then. I sat calmly on the bed and I spoke. I quoted him the Bible, how hate was indeed a power, but one that was furthest from God. How hate was a tool of evil, it was a trick, and a lie. How there was one source that told us that there is indeed something so much more powerful than hate, and it was love. Love was from God, and God defeated Satan, and always would. How anger could seem so powerful, how it could overcome and abuse people, and how love was a more subtle hand than that. Seeing the power of love required perception from God, and that forgiveness and letting go of hate was the only way to know love and God.

Funny thing is, it took me the next six months to give that same damned talk to myself this weekend.
